raw_graphql_pull_request.body:
## Motivation

A request may spend CPU time publishing its prefix cache after prefill and before output is streamed. Backend insertion work and blocking waits inside `checkpoint()` are not described by a CUDA copy event's DMA duration. Existing request traces do not identify that call, so a post-prefill gap cannot be separated from cache maintenance using the request timeline alone.

## Modifications

- Add the level-1 `cache_checkpoint_cpu` stage through the existing `ReqTimeStatsBase` and request trace APIs.
- Instrument prefix checkpoint calls through the scheduler's `checkpoint_kv_cache` and `release_kv_cache` helpers, covering ongoing requests and final KV-row release. Direct backend calls outside these helpers are not included. Keep skipped insertions and the tracing-disabled path unchanged; do not change cache admission, copying, scheduling, fences or metrics.
- Attach the phase, requested token boundary and normal-return status to the request's span. Capture monotonic timestamps immediately around the backend call and emit a completed span afterwards, so span construction/export is outside the measured interval.
- Keep tracing failures from skipping a checkpoint or replacing the backend's exception. Preserve the request's existing position/error behavior.
- Document that this is CPU call time. It can include shared backend waits and is not a count of copied tokens, GPU DMA time, Host/Store recovery proof or a cache-on/off end-to-end latency estimate. No device event or synchronization is introduced.

This complements, rather than replaces, transfer metrics and the outcome/structured-log work in #36474. It does not introduce another tracing exporter or request-ID Prometheus labels.

## Accuracy Tests

```bash
PYTHONPATH=python /path/to/venv/bin/python test/registered/unit/mem_cache/test_decode_radix_lock_ref.py
```

The existing registered CPU file passes with actual `Req`, `RadixCache`, CPU index rows, the existing allocator/pool test fixture and an OpenTelemetry in-memory span exporter. Added checks validate both checkpoint paths, the published prefix, request trace identity, balanced span closure, unchanged error propagation/position, and skipped/disabled behavior. The enabled path is run with `torch.cuda.synchronize` patched to fail if instrumentation adds a synchronization. The base revision still publishes the prefix but exports no checkpoint span, failing the added observability assertions.

The failure case injects an exception at the backend boundary; it does not claim to reproduce a physical GPU transfer failure. No server, pretrained model, GPU workload or external collector was started.

Follow-up self-review regressions fail on `e704cdb` and pass on this update. A controlled clock with a 2 ms backend interval and 250 ms of observer work previously produced a 252 ms cache span; the completed-span path reports only the 2 ms backend interval. These are deterministic fixture values, not GPU or production latency measurements. A real OpenTelemetry span processor failing at either `on_start` or `on_end` also verifies that successful prefix publication still completes and a backend exception retains its original type/message.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

This adds opt-in diagnostic spans, not an inference optimization. When tracing is disabled the call takes the existing checkpoint path after a boolean guard; no timestamp or device event is added. No GPU throughput, TTFT improvement, or quantitative production attribution is claimed. Existing synchronous and asynchronous trace APIs/exporters are reused. Span creation/export can still affect end-to-end latency when tracing is enabled; that observer overhead is deliberately excluded from this cache-call interval.

On current head `a6bd01d`, changed-file pre-commit checks and `mint broken-links` pass. On 2026-10-31 (Asia/Shanghai), full-site `CI=1 mint validate --format json` completed normally with exit code 0 in 89.339 seconds against a `git archive` snapshot of this exact head, using cached Mint 4.2.1178 / @mintlify/cli 4.0.1781. The report has `passed: true`, `build: {ran: true, passed: true}`, zero errors and six existing warnings. No validation rules or build steps were disabled.

The earlier limited runs and their post-timeout build output remain historical evidence; the normally completed isolated run now supplies current-head CLI exit status as well as build success. JSON/CI mode uses the non-interactive output path without publishing docs. This is local documentation validation, not upstream functional CI, fork-preview approval, or an inference performance result.

## Checklist

- [x] Format code with pre-commit.
- [x] Extend an existing registered CPU cache regression file.
- [x] Document the span and its interpretation in Production Request Tracing.
- [x] State the validation boundary and avoid unsupported performance claims.
- [x] Use existing tracing and cache conventions.

## Review and Merge Process

Maintainer review and upstream CI remain required. The local checks are not an upstream CI result or a production rollout.

@@ -70,6 +70,35 @@ This section explains how to configure the request tracing and export the trace
 
     **Note**: You must set the parameter `--enable-trace`; otherwise, the trace capability will not be enabled regardless of any dynamic adjustments to the trace level.
 
+## Cache checkpoint elapsed time
+
+With request tracing enabled at level 1 or higher, `cache_checkpoint_cpu` spans
+measure elapsed wall time around calls to the prefix cache's `checkpoint` method
+through the scheduler's
+`checkpoint_kv_cache` and `release_kv_cache` helpers. Direct backend calls outside
+these helpers are not instrumented by this stage.
+The span belongs to the request trace and carries:
+
+- `cache.checkpoint.phase`: `running` for an ongoing request, or `release` when
+  publishing a request's cache before releasing its KV row.
+- `cache.checkpoint.up_to`: the requested token boundary, not a count of newly
+  copied or retained tokens.
+- `cache.checkpoint.succeeded`: whether the checkpoint call returned normally.
+
+The interval is not CPU resource consumption: it includes insertion work and any
+blocking waits performed by
+the selected cache backend. Timestamps are captured around the backend call
+before creating or exporting the span, so tracing setup and export time are not
+included in this interval. Tracing can still affect end-to-end latency; the
+span does not measure that observer overhead. A tracing failure does not skip
+the cache call or replace its exception. The interval does not wait for an
+asynchronous copy just to
+measure it, and it is not GPU DMA time or proof of Host/Store recovery. A backend
+that drains shared work may include waits for other requests in this interval.
+Compare it with the request's prefill and output timeline; do not add overlapping
+CPU and GPU intervals or interpret this span alone as the end-to-end cost of
+enabling cache writes. Skipped cache insertions do not create checkpoint spans.
+
 ## Async Tracing (Reducing Performance Overhead)
 
 When batch sizes are large, synchronous OTel span creation can degrade inference throughput due to thread-safe locking and background export threads. Async tracing moves all span creation to a dedicated exporter process via ZMQ, keeping the scheduler and tokenizer hot paths free of OTel overhead.

+

+            patch.object(

+                            with self.assertRaisesRegex(ValueError, "copy failure"):
+                                checkpoint_kv_cache(req, cache)
+                        self.assertEqual(req.prefix_len, 0)
+                    else:
+                        checkpoint_kv_cache(req, cache)
+                        self.assertEqual(req.prefix_len, 4)
+                        result = cache.match_prefix(
+                            MatchPrefixParams(key=RadixKey(array("q", [1, 2, 3, 4])))
+                        )
+                        self.assertEqual(result.device_prefix_len, 4)
+                    req.time_stats.trace_ctx.trace_req_finish()
+
+
 if __name__ == "__main__":
     unittest.main()
